analysis.investment_thesis: K.V. Toys fails the Magic Formula on both axes: an earnings yield of ~3.7% (P/E 27.2) is far too expensive, and ROE of 1.01% implies a dismally low return on capital — nowhere near the >20% threshold. Cheap-and-good is the goal; this is expensive-and-poor.
key_strengths: Promoter holding of 58.34% shows reasonable skin-in-the-game
Some institutional interest (DII 8.03%) despite micro-cap status
key_risks: ROE of 1.01% signals near-zero return on capital — Magic Formula disqualifier
P/E of 27.2 = earnings yield ~3.7%, well below the 12% attractive threshold
Micro-cap (INR 124 Cr) in commoditized toy contract manufacturing with thin moat
red_flags: ROE ~1% — either margin collapse, over-capitalization, or near-zero earnings base
Paying 27x earnings for a sub-scale contract manufacturer is irrational
No disclosed EBIT/EV or ROIC data — but ROE of 1% makes ROIC almost certainly <5%
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The Magic Formula ranks companies on earnings yield (EBIT/EV) and return on capital. K.V. Toys fails both. A P/E of 27.2 translates to an earnings yield of roughly 3.7% — less than a government bond and one-fourth of what I'd consider attractive. Simultaneously, ROE of 1.01% tells me the business is barely generating any return on the capital deployed; even with modest leverage adjustments, ROIC is almost certainly in low single digits versus my 20%+ target. This is the textbook "expensive-and-bad" quadrant — the exact opposite of what the formula seeks.

Contract manufacturing of plastic and metal toys is a low-margin, commoditized business with little pricing power, competing against unorganized players and Chinese imports. There is no evidence of a durable moat, and the valuation reflects micro-cap SME-platform speculation rather than earnings power. I'd need to see ROIC expand above 20% AND the price fall by more than half before this screens anywhere near my universe. Pass decisively.
